content: Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) is a condition characterized by the spontaneous appearance of red, itchy, raised hives or wheals without any identifiable external trigger. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of H1-antihistamines in managing CSU. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared H1-antihistamines, either as monotherapy or in combination, against placebo or other active pharmacological treatments. The primary outcomes assessed were the complete suppression of urticaria, a good or excellent response, improvement in quality of life by 50% or more, and the occurrence of adverse events. A total of 73 studies involving 9759 participants were analyzed. The duration of treatment was categorized as short-term (up to two weeks) or intermediate-term (longer than two weeks, up to three months). The findings for specific H1-antihistamines are as follows: 1. Cetirizine: At a dose of 10 mg once daily, cetirizine was effective in achieving complete suppression of urticaria in both the short term and intermediate term compared to placebo (RR 2.72, 95% CI 1.51 to 4.91). 2. Desloratadine: At 5 mg daily in the intermediate term, desloratadine was more effective than placebo for complete suppression of urticaria (RR 37.00, 95% CI 2.31 to 593.70). At 20 mg daily in the short term, desloratadine also showed superiority over placebo (RR 15.97, 95% CI 1.04 to 245.04). No significant differences were observed between 5 mg and 10 mg doses for short-term treatment. 3. Levocetirizine: At 20 mg daily in the short term, levocetirizine was more effective than placebo for complete suppression of urticaria (RR 20.87, 95% CI 1.37 to 317.60). At 5 mg daily in the intermediate term, levocetirizine was effective (RR 52.88, 95% CI 3.31 to 843.81), but it was not effective at this dose in the short term. A 10 mg dose of levocetirizine was not effective in the short term. 4. Rupatadine: At doses of 10 mg and 20 mg in the intermediate term, rupatadine achieved a good or excellent response compared to placebo (RR 1.35, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.77). 5. Loratadine: At 10 mg daily, loratadine showed no significant difference compared to placebo for achieving a good or excellent response or complete suppression of urticaria in both the short term and intermediate term (RR 1.86, 95% CI 0.91 to 3.79). Comparisons of loratadine (10 mg) with cetirizine (10 mg), desloratadine (5 mg), mizolastine (10 mg), and emedastine (2 mg) in the intermediate term revealed no statistically significant differences in outcomes. No significant difference was observed between loratadine (10 mg) and hydroxyzine (25 mg) in the short term for complete suppression of urticaria (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.32 to 3.10). 6. Fexofenadine: When compared to cetirizine, fewer participants in the fexofenadine group achieved complete suppression of urticaria (P < 0.001). 7. Hydroxyzine: No significant differences in outcomes were observed between hydroxyzine (25 mg) and placebo in the intermediate term. Adverse events leading to withdrawal from treatment were not significantly different between active treatments and placebo in most comparisons. For example, cetirizine (10 mg and 20 mg), desloratadine (5 mg), loratadine (10 mg), mizolastine (10 mg), emedastine (2 mg), and hydroxyzine (25 mg) all showed no significant differences in withdrawal rates compared to placebo. The evidence for improvement in quality of life was insufficient across the studies. For example, no significant difference was observed between loratadine (10 mg) and mizolastine (10 mg) in the proportion of participants achieving at least a 50% improvement in quality of life (RR 3.21, 95% CI 0.32 to 32.33). In conclusion, while several H1-antihistamines demonstrated effectiveness in suppressing urticaria compared to placebo, the quality of evidence was generally low due to the small number of studies and limited sample sizes. Cetirizine at 10 mg once daily was found to be effective in both the short term and intermediate term. Desloratadine and levocetirizine also showed some efficacy, but the evidence was limited. No single H1-antihistamine emerged as the most effective treatment. Additionally, no significant differences in adverse events were observed between active treatments and placebo.
